Draw mg, mg sin(theta) and mg cos(theta) as three separate forces.
Assume zero perpendicular acceleration means zero total acceleration.
Assume N=mg on a tilted surface.
Point friction automatically uphill or downhill without first checking the slip tendency.

questions.stem: An ice-hockey puck of mass 0.2 kg slides across smooth ice at 4 m/s after the stick loses contact. Friction and air resistance are negligible. What horizontal forces act on it, what is its velocity 3 s later, and would a puck at rest on the same ice start moving?
conditions: Friction and air resistance are negligible.
The ice is horizontal.

answer.summary: No horizontal force acts. The puck still moves at 4 m/s, having covered 12 m, and a puck at rest stays at rest.
reasoning: Once the stick loses contact, nothing touches the puck horizontally, so the horizontal net force is zero.
F_net = m a gives a = 0/0.2 = 0 m/s², so the velocity does not change: after 3 s it is still 4 m/s.
Equal times give equal advances: 4 m in each second, 12 m in 3 s.
A puck at rest under the same zero net force keeps its zero velocity, so it stays at rest.
answer.check: With even a small friction force added, the puck would slow down: the force changes the velocity rather than keeping it up.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg lamp hangs at rest from a ceiling cord. Take g = 10 m/s² and up as positive. List each force on the lamp with its size, find the net force, and say what would happen if the cord were cut.
conditions: The lamp is at rest.
The cord is light and vertical.

answer.summary: The cord pulls up with 15 N and gravity pulls down with 15 N; the net force is zero. If the cord were cut, the lamp would accelerate downward at 10 m/s².
reasoning: Two agents act on the lamp: the Earth, through its weight, and the cord, through its tension.
Weight: 1.5 × 10 = 15 N, so −15 N on the declared axis.
The lamp is at rest, so F_net = 0: T − 15 = 0 and T = +15 N. Both forces are real and non-zero.
Cut the cord and only the weight remains: F_net = −15 N and a = −15/1.5 = −10 m/s².
answer.check: The cut-cord case shows that the 15 N weight was acting all along; the tension had been cancelling it, not removing it.

questions.stem: A 50 kg child stands on a 20 kg box that rests on the floor. Take g = 10 m/s². Build the free-body inventory of the box: name each force, its agent, its direction and its size.
conditions: Everything is at rest.
The floor is horizontal.

answer.summary: On the box: its weight 200 N down (Earth), the child's push 500 N down (child), and the floor's push 700 N up (floor). The child's own weight is not on the box's diagram.
reasoning: Chosen body: the box. Every arrow must answer 'who acts on the box?'.
Earth on box: weight 20 × 10 = 200 N down. Child on box: a contact push down; the child is at rest, so it equals the child's weight, 500 N.
Floor on box: the box is at rest, so the floor pushes up with 200 + 500 = 700 N.
The child's 500 N weight acts on the child, and the box's 500 N upward push acts on the child too; both belong on the child's diagram.
answer.check: Taking child and box together, the floor supports a total weight of 700 N, the same floor force the box's own diagram gives.

questions.stem: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in a lift that accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Take g = 10 m/s² and up as positive. Find the scale reading using the ground frame, then again using the lift frame with a pseudo-force, and compare.
conditions: The ground frame is treated as inertial.
The person stays in contact with the scale.

answer.summary: Both descriptions give a scale reading of 720 N.
reasoning: Ground frame: the physical forces are the scale's push N up and the weight 600 N down, and the person accelerates at +2 m/s².
Ground-frame equation: N − 600 = 60 × 2, so N = 720 N.
Lift frame: the person is at rest, and the frame accelerates at +2 m/s², so add F_pseudo = −m a_frame = −120 N.
Lift-frame equation: N − 600 − 120 = 0, so N = 720 N, the same reading.
answer.check: With the lift at rest or moving steadily, a_frame = 0, the pseudo-force vanishes and both frames give N = 600 N.

questions.stem: A 10 kg crate is pulled up a smooth ramp inclined at 30° by a rope parallel to the ramp with a force of 70 N. Take g = 10 m/s². Using axes along and perpendicular to the ramp, find the crate's acceleration and the normal force, and the pull that would give zero acceleration.
conditions: The ramp is fixed and smooth.
The crate stays in contact with the ramp.

answer.summary: a = 2 m/s² up the ramp, N ≈ 86.6 N, and a 50 N pull would give zero acceleration.
reasoning: Body: the crate. +x up the ramp, +y out of the ramp. Forces: the 70 N pull along +x, the 100 N weight vertically down, the normal force N along +y.
Resolve the weight: 100 × sin 30° = 50 N down the ramp and 100 × cos 30° ≈ 86.6 N into the ramp.
Along the ramp: F_net = 70 − 50 = 20 N, so a = 20/10 = 2 m/s² up the ramp.
Across the ramp the crate keeps contact, so a_y = 0 and N ≈ 86.6 N. A 50 N pull would make F_net = 0 along the ramp, so a = 0.
answer.check: Units: 20 N / 10 kg = 2 m/s². On level ground (0°) the same method gives N = 100 N and no down-slope weight component.

questions.stem: In space, a 70 kg astronaut pushes a 350 kg satellite with a force of 140 N. During the push, find the force on each body and each body's acceleration.
conditions: No other forces act during the push.
Use an inertial frame in which both start at rest.

answer.summary: Each body feels 140 N, in opposite directions: the satellite accelerates at 0.4 m/s² away from the astronaut, and the astronaut at 2 m/s² the other way.
reasoning: The interaction is the contact between hand and satellite: astronaut on satellite and satellite on astronaut.
Astronaut on satellite: 140 N, on the satellite's diagram. Satellite on astronaut: 140 N the opposite way, on the astronaut's diagram.
Satellite: a = 140/350 = 0.4 m/s².
Astronaut: a = 140/70 = 2 m/s², in the opposite direction. Neither diagram contains both forces, so they do not cancel.
answer.check: Mass times acceleration gives 350 × 0.4 = 140 N and 70 × 2 = 140 N: both equal the one shared interaction force.

questions.stem: A book rests on a tray. A waiter first carries the tray at steady speed in a straight line, then speeds up forward; the book never slips. Find the friction force of the tray on the book in each stage, including whether it can be zero.
conditions: The book does not slip on the tray at any time.
The tray stays horizontal.

answer.summary: During the steady carry the friction is zero; while the tray speeds up, static friction on the book points forward.
reasoning: Choose the book as the body; the contact is the tray's top surface, and friction acts along it.
Steady carry: if the tray became perfectly slippery, the book would keep moving with the tray, so there is no slip tendency and the friction is zero.
Speeding up: without friction the book would keep its old speed while the tray moved ahead, so the book would slip backward relative to the tray.
Static friction opposes that tendency, so the tray's friction on the book points forward, the same way the book is moving.
answer.check: The book speeds up forward and friction is the only horizontal force on it, so by F_net = m a that force must point forward, which agrees.

questions.stem: A 4 kg box rests on a rough horizontal floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4. Take g = 10 m/s². A horizontal pull of 15 N is applied, and in a second trial a pull of 25 N. For each trial decide whether the box stays at rest, and find the friction force and the acceleration.
conditions: The pull is horizontal in both trials.
The box starts at rest each time.

answer.summary: At 15 N the box stays at rest with 15 N of static friction. At 25 N it slides, kinetic friction is 16 N, and the acceleration is 2.25 m/s².
reasoning: Vertical balance gives N = mg = 4 × 10 = 40 N, so static friction can supply at most μ_s N = 0.5 × 40 = 20 N.
15 N trial: rest would need friction of 15 N, and 15 N ≤ 20 N, so the box stays at rest with f_s = 15 N and a = 0.
25 N trial: rest would need 25 N of friction, more than the 20 N available, so the box slides.
Once sliding, f_k = μ_k N = 0.4 × 40 = 16 N against the motion, so a = (25 − 16)/4 = 2.25 m/s² in the direction of the pull.
answer.check: Had friction been set to 20 N in the 15 N trial, the net force would be 5 N backward on a box at rest, which static friction can never produce.

questions.stem: Blocks A (3 kg) and B (2 kg) touch on a smooth floor, A to the left of B. A 20 N force pushes A to the right into B, and a 5 N force pushes B to the left, back toward A. The blocks stay in contact. Write one Newton-II equation per block and solve for their acceleration and the contact force.
conditions: The floor is frictionless.
Take rightward as positive.
The blocks stay in contact.

answer.summary: The blocks accelerate together at 3 m/s² to the right, and the contact force between them is 11 N.
reasoning: Maintained contact fixes the separation of A and B, so with rightward positive a_A = a_B = a.
For A: the 20 N push acts right and B pushes back on A with the contact force N, so 20 − N = 3a.
For B: A pushes B right with N and the 5 N force acts left, so N − 5 = 2a.
Adding the equations removes N: 15 = 5a, so a = 3 m/s². Then N = 5 + 2 × 3 = 11 N.
answer.check: Check A on its own: 20 − 11 = 9 N, and 3 kg × 3 m/s² = 9 N.

questions.stem: A 2 kg bucket hangs from a light rope tied under a 1 kg bucket. A second rope lifts the top bucket with a 45 N upward force. Take g = 10 m/s² and up as positive. Choose a system to find the acceleration, then a different system to find the tension in the rope between the buckets.
conditions: The ropes are light and stay taut.
Both buckets move together vertically.

answer.summary: The buckets accelerate upward at 5 m/s², and the rope between them carries 30 N.
reasoning: For the acceleration, take both buckets as one system: the connecting rope's pulls are internal and drop out.
External forces on the system: 45 N up and weight (1 + 2) × 10 = 30 N down, so 45 − 30 = 3a and a = 5 m/s².
For the connecting rope, isolate the lower bucket: that rope's pull is external to it.
Lower bucket: T − 2 × 10 = 2 × 5, so T = 30 N.
answer.check: Check the top bucket alone: 45 − 10 − 30 = 5 N, and 1 kg × 5 m/s² = 5 N.

questions.stem: A light, taut, inextensible string runs from a 2 kg cart on a smooth table, over a frictionless light pulley at the table's edge, down to a 1 kg hanging mass. Take g = 10 m/s². State the model that allows one tension T, list the forces on each body, and find the acceleration and T.
conditions: The table is frictionless.
The pulley is light and frictionless.

answer.summary: One T is allowed by the ideal string and pulley. The acceleration is 10/3 ≈ 3.33 m/s² and T = 20/3 ≈ 6.67 N.
reasoning: The string is light, taut and inextensible and the pulley is light and frictionless, so one tension T acts along the whole string.
On the cart: T pulls it toward the pulley; its weight and the table's normal force balance vertically.
On the hanging mass: T pulls it up and its 10 N weight pulls it down; both bodies share one acceleration magnitude a.
Cart: T = 2a. Hanging mass, down positive: 10 − T = 1 × a. Adding gives 10 = 3a, so a = 10/3 m/s² and T = 20/3 N.
answer.check: T ≈ 6.67 N is less than the 10 N weight, as it must be for a mass that accelerates downward.

questions.stem: A 2 kg lamp hangs from a light cord inside a lift. Take up as positive and g = 10 m/s². Find the cord tension when the lift (a) moves up at steady speed, (b) accelerates upward at 2 m/s², and (c) accelerates downward at 3 m/s².
conditions: The lamp moves with the lift.
The cord is light and stays taut.

answer.summary: The tension is 20 N, 24 N and 14 N in the three cases.
reasoning: Only the cord and the lamp's weight act on the lamp, and nothing makes the cord non-ideal, so T comes from the lamp's own equation: T − 20 = 2a.
(a) Steady speed means a = 0, so T = 20 N.
answer.check: In free fall, a = −10 m/s², the same equation gives T = 20 − 20 = 0: the cord goes slack, as expected.

questions.stem: One taut inextensible string passes over a fixed pulley and holds A and B. With y_A and y_B measured downward from the pulley along each segment, y_A = 1.2 m and y_B = 0.8 m. A then moves down by 0.3 m. Find B's new position, and B's velocity at an instant when A moves down at 0.5 m/s.
conditions: The pulley is fixed.
The string stays taut and does not stretch.

answer.summary: B rises to y_B = 0.5 m; when A moves down at 0.5 m/s, v_B = −0.5 m/s, that is 0.5 m/s upward.
reasoning: Both coordinates are measured away from the pulley, so the changing length is y_A + y_B = 1.2 + 0.8 = 2.0 m, fixed.
After A moves down 0.3 m, y_A = 1.5 m, so y_B = 2.0 − 1.5 = 0.5 m: B has risen 0.3 m.
Differentiating y_A + y_B = 2.0 m gives v_A + v_B = 0.
With v_A = +0.5 m/s, v_B = −0.5 m/s: B moves toward the pulley at 0.5 m/s.
answer.check: The new lengths 1.5 m and 0.5 m still add to 2.0 m, so the string has neither stretched nor gone slack.

questions.stem: Masses A (3 kg) and B (1 kg) hang from one light inextensible string over a fixed, frictionless, light pulley, with y_A and y_B measured downward from the pulley. Take g = 10 m/s². Using a_A + a_B = 0 and one tension T, find a_A, a_B and T, and name the assumption each of those two relations rests on.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
The string stays taut.

answer.summary: a_A = +5 m/s² (down), a_B = −5 m/s² (up) and T = 15 N. The acceleration relation rests on the fixed string length; the single T rests on the ideal pulley and string.
reasoning: The fixed total length gives a_A + a_B = 0 in these coordinates; this uses geometry only.
One tension T is licensed separately, because the string is light and the pulley is light and frictionless.
Down positive for each mass: A: 30 − T = 3a_A. B: 10 − T = 1 × a_B = −a_A.
Subtracting B's equation from A's: 20 = 4a_A, so a_A = 5 m/s², a_B = −5 m/s², and T = 30 − 3 × 5 = 15 N.
answer.check: As one system driven by the weight difference, (3 − 1) × 10 = 20 N on 4 kg gives 5 m/s², matching the two body equations.

questions.stem: A 4 kg body has a net external force of +12 N along a declared axis. Find its acceleration.

answer.summary: The acceleration is +3 m/s^2.
reasoning: Use F_net = m a for the chosen body.
The positive sign matches the net-force direction.
answer.check: Multiplying 4 kg by +3 m/s^2 recovers +12 N.

hints.text: Start by asking: Which body are we solving for?
Add all signed external forces first; acceleration follows the net force, not an isolated arrow.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the body as a dot on the declared axis with a single arrow for the +12 N net force.

questions.failure_signal: Your answer is 48 m/s² or 1/3 m/s²: F_net = m a means dividing the net force by the mass, 12/4, not multiplying them or dividing the other way.

family_exposure.closure: Established: with the net force known, a = F_net/m, pointing along the net force. The transfer task sets up the same law on an incline in two different choices of axes.

questions.stem: One cart is at rest and another moves steadily in a straight line. For each, decide whether zero net force is compatible with the motion and explain the common rule.

answer.summary: Zero net force is compatible with both. Each cart can keep its current velocity unchanged.
reasoning: Rest is a zero velocity that stays zero.
Steady straight motion is a nonzero velocity that stays unchanged.
The shared condition is no change of velocity, not no motion.
answer.check: Ask whether the motion description contains speeding up, slowing down, or turning. If none occurs, zero net force remains compatible.

hints.text: Start by asking yourself: After the hand leaves the cart, is the hand still exerting the forward push?
Separate velocity from change of velocity: a net force is required for acceleration, not for the existence of motion.

hint_ladder.text: Draw each cart with its velocity arrow and, separately, its net-force arrow; leave the net-force arrow empty if nothing changes that cart's velocity.

questions.failure_signal: You said the moving cart needs a forward force to keep going: that confuses having a velocity with changing it; steady straight motion needs zero net force, just as rest does.

family_exposure.closure: Established: zero net force means an unchanging velocity, and rest is the case where that velocity is zero. Later tasks read steady straight motion as a balanced-force state.

questions.stem: An object has two equal opposite forces acting on it. Explain what is zero and what is not, then state what motion change the net result predicts.

answer.summary: The net force is zero, but both individual forces are nonzero. The zero net result predicts no change of velocity.
reasoning: Each force remains an actual interaction on the body.
Opposite equal directional effects cancel only when combined.
A zero net force is consistent with unchanged velocity.
answer.check: Increase both forces equally; the net remains zero even though neither individual force disappears.

hints.text: Start by asking: Before adding anything, how many pushes are physically acting on the box?
List every interaction force on the body, then combine their directions; cancellation belongs to the net result, not to the individual forces.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the object with both arrows at full length, then write their signed sum beside the diagram without erasing either arrow.

questions.failure_signal: You wrote that no forces act: both forces are present and non-zero; only their sum is zero.

family_exposure.closure: Established: forces can be real and non-zero while their sum is zero, and it is the sum that sets the change of velocity. Later tasks keep every force listed on a free-body diagram before any are combined.

questions.stem: A person pushes a box. Describe the two contact-force partner arrows and state which one belongs on the box's free-body diagram.

answer.summary: The person's force on the box belongs on the box diagram. The box's equal-and-opposite force on the person belongs on the person's diagram.
reasoning: Choose the box first.
Ask which member of the contact pair acts on the box.
The partner acts on the person, so it cannot cancel the first force on the box diagram.
answer.check: Switch the chosen body to the person; the membership of the two partner arrows must switch with it.

hints.text: Start by asking: Which single body are you describing first?
Choose one body first. Put only forces acting on that body on its diagram; draw the partner force only when the other body is chosen.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the box and the person as two separate outlines, then draw each contact force on the outline of the body it acts on.

questions.failure_signal: You put both partner arrows on the box and let them cancel: the box's push on the person acts on the person, so it cannot be part of the box's sum.

family_exposure.closure: Established: a diagram holds only the forces on its own body, so a partner force never cancels on it. The transfer task finds the same kind of double count hidden in resolved components on an incline.

questions.stem: A box is placed on a conveyor belt moving to the right faster than the box. Before the box matches the belt speed, what direction is the friction force on the box?

answer.summary: The friction force on the box points to the right.
reasoning: Relative to the belt, the box tends to slip left at the contact.
Friction opposes that relative slip tendency.
Therefore the belt's friction on the box points right and accelerates it.
answer.check: The answer is allowed to point with the box's motion because friction is defined by the contact slip tendency, not by the box's velocity alone.

hints.text: Start by asking: Which two surfaces are in contact?
Decide the relative sliding tendency at the contact first; friction opposes that tendency.

hint_ladder.text: Draw only the box and the belt surface, with an arrow for how fast each moves. Mark which way the box would slide relative to the belt if the contact were perfectly slippery.

questions.failure_signal: Your friction arrow points left because the box 'lags behind': that is the way the box slips relative to the belt, and friction points the opposite way, to the right.

family_exposure.closure: Established: friction's direction comes from the slip tendency at the contact, not from the object's velocity. The transfer task applies the same rule to a shoe pushing on the ground.

questions.stem: A swimmer pushes water backward. Identify the third-law partner force and state which body each force acts on.

answer.summary: The swimmer pushes the water backward, and the water pushes the swimmer forward with an equal-magnitude opposite force. The two forces act on different bodies.
reasoning: The interaction is swimmer-water contact.
Swimmer on water acts on the water.
Water on swimmer acts on the swimmer in the opposite direction.
answer.check: Only the water-on-swimmer force belongs on the swimmer's free-body diagram.

hints.text: Start by asking: What is the interaction?
No. Put each partner on the body it acts on; only then sum forces for one body.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the swimmer and a parcel of water as two separate outlines, and label each arrow 'swimmer on water' or 'water on swimmer'.

questions.failure_signal: You said the two forces cancel, so the swimmer cannot move: they act on different bodies, and the swimmer's own sum contains only the water's forward push.

family_exposure.closure: Established: third-law partners are equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so each belongs to a different body's sum. Later tasks keep interaction pairs apart in connected-body problems.

questions.stem: Plan a trolley–pulley–hanging-mass experiment to verify Newton’s second law. Describe one controlled variation that tests the effect of net force at fixed system mass, what you measure, and what result would support F_net = m a.
conditions: Treat friction as small or measure/account for it consistently.
Use the same trolley–pulley system while changing the driving load.

answer.summary: Keep the total moving mass approximately fixed while transferring masses between trolley and hanger so the driving force changes, measure acceleration for each trial, and test whether acceleration changes in direct proportion to the corrected net driving force.
reasoning: Choose the trolley plus hanging mass as the moving system and keep its total mass fixed for the force-variation test.
Move a known mass from trolley to hanger to increase the driving weight without changing total moving mass.
Measure acceleration from distance/time data or a suitable motion sensor for each trial.
Correct for friction consistently if it is not negligible.
For fixed total mass, a plot of corrected F_net against a should be approximately linear through the origin within experimental uncertainty.
answer.check: Changing force and total mass at the same time without controlling either would not isolate the F_net–a relationship.

hints.text: To test the effect of force, do not let total moving mass become a second uncontrolled variable.
Transfer masses between the trolley and hanger, then compare corrected net force with measured acceleration.

hint_ladder.text: Sketch the trolley on the bench, the string over the pulley and the hanger, and draw one boundary around trolley plus hanger: the mass inside it must stay fixed.

questions.failure_signal: Your plan adds new masses to the hanger from outside: then the driving force and the moving mass both change, so a change in acceleration cannot be put down to force alone.

family_exposure.closure: Established: to test F_net = m a, vary the net driving force while the system mass stays fixed, by moving masses between trolley and hanger. Later tasks use the same system boundary to find the acceleration of connected bodies.

questions.stem: A small block of mass m rests on a larger block of mass M. The floor under the larger block is smooth. A horizontal force F is applied to the larger block. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is mu_s. Derive the largest value of F for which the two blocks can move together without slipping.
conditions: The upper block has no other horizontal force.
The contact surfaces remain horizontal.
Use the static-friction limit only at impending slip.

answer.summary: While there is no slip, both blocks have a = F/(M+m). The upper block needs friction f_required = m a. Since N = m g here, no slip requires mF/(M+m) <= mu_s m g, so F <= mu_s(M+m)g. Therefore F_max = mu_s(M+m)g.
reasoning: Treat both blocks together first: the only external horizontal force on the two-block system is F, so a = F/(M+m).
For the upper block alone, static friction is the horizontal force that must provide acceleration a, so f_required = m a = mF/(M+m).
Because the contact is horizontal with no other vertical force on the upper block, N = m g.
Static contact is possible only while f_required <= mu_s N; equality occurs at impending slip.
Substituting and cancelling m gives F_max = mu_s(M+m)g.
answer.check: For F below this threshold, the required friction is below its maximum; setting f_s = mu_s N for every smaller F would incorrectly predict the same friction at all forces.

hints.text: First suppose the blocks do not slip. What acceleration would the two-block system then have?
Now isolate only the upper block. What horizontal force must accelerate it at that same rate? Compare that required friction with the static limit.

hint_ladder.text: Draw one diagram for each block. On the upper block the only horizontal force is the friction from the lower block; on the lower block, F and the partner of that friction.

questions.failure_signal: Your answer is F_max = μ_s m g: that is the friction limit itself, but F must accelerate both blocks, so the limit is scaled up by (M + m)/m.

family_exposure.closure: Established: for a no-slip threshold, find the shared acceleration from the whole system, then test the friction one block needs against μ_s N. The transfer task leaves the contact state open, so you must first decide whether rest can hold at all.

questions.stem: Two blocks A and B of masses m_A and m_B remain in contact on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force F pushes A toward B, and the contact is maintained. Derive their common acceleration and the magnitude of the contact force exerted by A on B.
conditions: The floor is frictionless.
The blocks remain in contact throughout the motion.
Take the direction of F as positive.

answer.summary: The fixed contact keeps the blocks at one common acceleration a = F/(m_A+m_B). For block B alone, the contact force is its only horizontal force, so N_AB = m_B a = m_B F/(m_A+m_B).
reasoning: Because the maintained contact fixes the separation of A and B along the motion direction, they share one acceleration component.
For the combined system A+B, the contact pair is internal and the external horizontal force is F, giving a = F/(m_A+m_B).
For B alone, the force exerted by A is external to B and must remain on B's free-body diagram.
Newton II for B gives N_AB = m_B a = m_B F/(m_A+m_B).
answer.check: If m_B tends to zero, the required contact force tends to zero while the system acceleration tends to F/m_A, which is consistent.

hints.text: What physical condition lets you use one acceleration for both blocks?
Find the acceleration from the combined system first. Then isolate B; do not cancel the contact force from B's own equation.

hint_ladder.text: Draw A and B as two separate diagrams with the contact pair between them, then draw one dashed outline around both blocks.

questions.failure_signal: Your contact force equals F: the push on A is not passed to B undiminished, because part of F accelerates A itself; B needs only m_B a.

family_exposure.closure: Established: maintained contact gives one acceleration, the whole system finds it, and the body that feels a contact force is isolated to find that force. The transfer task adds a third cart and leaves the choice of system to you.

questions.stem: Two carts A and B of masses m_A and m_B are connected by one taut massless inextensible string on a smooth horizontal track. A horizontal force F pulls cart A away from B along the string. Derive the common acceleration and the string tension. Then name one model change that would make equal tension throughout the connector no longer guaranteed.
conditions: The string is massless, taut and inextensible.
There is no pulley in this question.
The track is frictionless.

answer.summary: The string constraint gives one acceleration a = F/(m_A+m_B). For B, T = m_B a, so T = m_B F/(m_A+m_B). Equal tension relies on the ideal massless-string model; a connector with significant mass or a nonideal redirection can invalidate one common T.
reasoning: The taut inextensible connector keeps the cart separation fixed, so their acceleration components along the track are equal.
Treating A+B as one system gives F = (m_A+m_B)a.
For B alone, the only horizontal force is the string tension, so T = m_B a.
Substitution gives T = m_B F/(m_A+m_B).
Using one tension magnitude is a model consequence, not a universal property of every rope or pulley arrangement.
answer.check: The tension is smaller than F for positive m_A and m_B, because part of F accelerates cart A as well as cart B.
acceptable_alternatives: A massive string, an elastic connector with a nonuniform dynamical model, or a frictional/inertial pulley in a redirected setup are valid examples of a model change that can invalidate equal tension.

hints.text: State the connector model before using one symbol T. What does taut and inextensible imply about the two cart accelerations?
Use the whole two-cart system to find a, then isolate B to find the tension acting on B.

hint_ladder.text: Draw cart A and cart B separately. Put the string's pull on each, along the string away from that cart, and give both the symbol T only after naming the ideal-string assumptions.

questions.failure_signal: Your tension equals F: the string has only to accelerate cart B, so T = m_B a, which is less than F.

family_exposure.closure: Established: an ideal taut string gives one acceleration and one tension, and the tension comes from the body it pulls. The transfer task breaks one ideal assumption, a rough pulley axle, and asks what survives.

questions.stem: One taut inextensible string passes over one fixed pulley. Let y_A and y_B be the two straight segment lengths measured positive away from the pulley. Write the string-length relation and derive the corresponding velocity and acceleration relations. If A accelerates away from the pulley with magnitude a, state B's signed acceleration in these coordinates.
conditions: The pulley is fixed.
Only the two declared straight string segments change length.
The string remains taut and inextensible.

answer.summary: The variable string length obeys y_A + y_B = constant. Therefore v_A + v_B = 0 and a_A + a_B = 0. If a_A = +a away from the pulley, then a_B = -a, toward the pulley.
reasoning: For one fixed pulley, the wrapped/fixed part of the string contributes no changing length in this bounded geometry.
Inextensibility makes the sum of the two changing straight segment lengths constant.
Taking one and two time derivatives gives the velocity and acceleration constraints.
With both coordinates positive away from the pulley, the signed accelerations are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
answer.check: If both y_A and y_B increased together, total string length would increase, contradicting inextensibility.

hints.text: Which parts of the string can change length while the pulley itself stays fixed?
Write the sum of those changing segments as a constant before thinking about velocities or accelerations.

hint_ladder.text: Sketch the pulley and the two straight segments, and label y_A and y_B as lengths measured from the pulley along each segment.

questions.failure_signal: You wrote a_A = a_B: measured away from the pulley, one segment lengthens while the other shortens, so the signed accelerations must be opposite.

family_exposure.closure: Established: one fixed pulley and one inextensible string give y_A + y_B = constant, so a_A + a_B = 0 in away-from-pulley coordinates. The transfer task gives the geometry in words with upward coordinates, so the length relation must be rebuilt.

questions.stem: A bus accelerates to the right on a straight road. A loose object on a smooth horizontal shelf is described first by a roadside observer and then by a passenger in the bus. Explain how the two descriptions differ and where, if anywhere, a pseudo-force is used.
conditions: The roadside frame is treated as inertial.
The bus has nonzero rightward acceleration.
The object-shelf friction is negligible.

answer.summary: The roadside description uses only physical interactions; the loose object does not acquire a new backward physical force merely because the bus accelerates. In the accelerating bus frame, a backward pseudo-force may be introduced as a modelling convention so Newton's laws can be written in that non-inertial frame.
reasoning: Changing observer does not create a new physical agent acting on the loose object.
The roadside observer can describe the object with the physical forces only.
The passenger's frame accelerates with the bus, so relative to that observer the object appears to shift backward.
A backward pseudo-force is added only in the accelerating-frame description if that convention is used.
answer.check: If the bus later moves at constant velocity, changing from roadside to bus observer does not by itself require a pseudo-force.

hints.text: Ask first whether any new physical object began touching or attracting the loose object when the bus started accelerating.
Identify which observer is accelerating before deciding whether an extra convention is needed.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the bus and the object twice, once labelled 'roadside' and once 'passenger', each with that observer's own acceleration arrow.

questions.failure_signal: You gave the object a backward physical force in the roadside account: nothing new touches it; the backward term exists only in the passenger's accelerating description.

family_exposure.closure: Established: an inertial observer uses physical forces only, and an accelerating observer adds −m a_frame. The transfer task asks you to choose the frame yourself from what the description must achieve.

questions.stem: A crate rests on a rough horizontal floor. It is pulled by a force P at an upward angle theta. The coefficients mu_s and mu_k are known, but the statement does not say whether the crate slips. For a specified P, determine the crate's acceleration or justify that it remains at rest.
conditions: Resolve the applied force into horizontal and vertical components.
The crate remains in contact with the floor.
Do not assume a friction equality before deciding the contact state.

answer.summary: First find N = mg - P sin(theta). Under a provisional no-slip state, the friction required is f_required = P cos(theta). If |f_required| <= mu_s N, the crate can remain at rest and static friction equals the required value. If that inequality fails, sliding occurs; then use kinetic friction mu_k N opposite the sliding and apply Newton II to find acceleration.
reasoning: The upward component of P changes the normal reaction, so N is not automatically mg.
The coefficient data do not identify the contact state; test the static state first.
Compare the no-slip friction requirement with the static limit.
Only after the static state is impossible is the kinetic-friction model selected for the acceleration calculation.
answer.check: At P=0, the method must allow friction to be zero rather than mu_s mg.

rubric.criterion: Computes the actual normal reaction before any friction limit.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizes that friction limits depend on the contact force, not a memorized N=mg shortcut.

rubric.criterion: Tests the no-slip friction requirement against mu_s N before choosing a kinetic model.
rubric.evidence_of: Can select the contact model rather than treating a supplied coefficient as an instruction to use equality.

rubric.criterion: Uses kinetic friction only after static feasibility fails.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps static and sliding contact states distinct.

hints.text: The presence of mu_s and mu_k does not tell you which one to use. What contact state would you test first?
Before deciding the friction model, ask whether the vertical component of the pull changes the normal reaction.

transfer.invariant: The normal force from the actual force balance, the provisional no-slip requirement and its comparison with μ_s N all carry over; what changes is that the contact state is not given and must be decided.

Without being told which system to choose, find the acceleration of the three-cart train and the contact force that B exerts on C.
conditions: The carts remain in contact.
The track is frictionless.
Take the direction of F as positive.

answer.summary: Use A+B+C as one system for the acceleration: a = F/(3m). Then isolate C to find the requested contact force: N_BC = m a = F/3. The B-on-C force is internal only to the three-cart system; it is external to cart C and must remain in C's equation.
reasoning: Maintained contact gives the carts one common acceleration along the track.
For the acceleration, the whole three-cart system removes internal contact forces from the summed equation.
For the requested B-on-C contact force, isolate C because that interaction is external to C.
Newton II on C gives N_BC = mF/(3m) = F/3.
answer.check: Cancelling B-on-C while solving cart C alone would leave C with no horizontal force but nonzero acceleration, which is inconsistent.

rubric.evidence_of: Can select a system boundary that removes irrelevant internal forces.

A proposed solution writes the same tension T on both sides of the pulley before doing any calculation. Decide whether that step is justified by the Grade9V3 ideal-string model and explain what can still be said without introducing a new pulley model.

The pulley axle is not frictionless.
No quantitative nonideal-pulley relation is supplied.

A quantitative solution would require an additional model that is outside this slice.
reasoning: Tension forces still belong on the bodies they act on.
Uniform tension across a redirection was licensed only after declaring a frictionless, massless ideal pulley/string model.
Appreciable axle friction breaks that declared model condition.
Therefore equal tension cannot be imported; the correct bounded response is to stop rather than manufacture a nonideal relation.

questions.stem: A diagram is replaced by this verbal description: one taut inextensible string passes over one fixed pulley, with mass A on the left end and mass B on the right end. Coordinates x_A and x_B are both defined positive upward. Before writing any Newton-II equations, construct the string-length relation and derive the signed acceleration relation in these coordinates.
conditions: The pulley is fixed.
Only the two vertical straight string segments change length.
Both coordinates are positive upward, toward the pulley.

answer.summary: Because the changing segment lengths decrease when x_A or x_B increases, the variable string length can be written (C_A - x_A) + (C_B - x_B) = constant. Hence x_A + x_B = constant, so v_A + v_B = 0 and a_A + a_B = 0. Thus if A accelerates upward, B accelerates downward with equal magnitude.
reasoning: Translate the verbal geometry into the two changing string-segment lengths.
The chosen coordinates are upward, so each segment length is a constant offset minus its coordinate.
Inextensibility makes the sum of the segment lengths constant.
Differentiating the equivalent x_A + x_B = constant relation gives the signed velocity and acceleration constraints.
answer.check: If both masses accelerated upward in these coordinates, both vertical segments would shorten and the fixed total string length would be violated.

A student wants the bob to be at rest in the chosen coordinates while finding the string direction. Decide which observer description makes that possible, state the extra modelling term required there, and give an independent inertial-frame alternative without solving for a numerical angle.

The car acceleration is constant and nonzero.
Air resistance is neglected.

Alternatively, use the roadside inertial frame with only physical forces and give the bob the same rightward acceleration as the car. Both descriptions must predict the same string direction.

Because that observer frame accelerates, Newton's second law there needs the backward pseudo-force convention.
In the roadside inertial frame no pseudo-force is added; the bob has the car's horizontal acceleration.
The two descriptions are alternative models of the same physical situation and must agree on the observable string direction.

questions.stem: A crate rests on a rough horizontal floor. No horizontal force acts on it, and there is no tendency for the crate to slide relative to the floor. What is the friction force on the crate?
conditions: The crate remains at rest.
No other horizontal interaction acts on the crate.

answer.summary: The friction force is zero.
reasoning: Friction responds to relative sliding or a tendency to slide at the contact.
Here no horizontal force or other effect creates a tangential slip tendency.
Therefore no tangential contact force is required, so f=0.
answer.check: Roughness provides the ability to supply friction when needed; it does not require a nonzero friction force in every contact state.

hints.text: Ask what relative sliding or slip tendency would appear at the contact if friction were absent.
If no tangential force is required to prevent relative sliding, the friction value need not be nonzero.

hint_ladder.text: Sketch the crate and list every horizontal force you can name. If the list is empty, ask what a friction force would have to balance.

questions.failure_signal: You gave a non-zero friction such as μ_s mg: nothing pushes the crate sideways, so there is no slip tendency and nothing for friction to oppose.

family_exposure.closure: Established: a rough contact supplies friction only when a slip tendency needs opposing, so a crate at rest with no sideways force has f = 0. The transfer task keeps this rule for a crate that moves together with its platform.

questions.stem: A 5 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor. A 12 N horizontal pull is applied, but the block remains at rest. The coefficient of static friction is 0.6 and take g=10 m/s^2. Find the actual static friction and its limiting value.
conditions: The pull is horizontal.
The block remains at rest.

answer.summary: The actual static friction is 12 N opposite the pull; the limiting value is 30 N.
reasoning: Because the block remains at rest, the horizontal net force is zero.
Static friction therefore supplies the 12 N needed to balance the pull, rather than automatically taking its maximum value.
The vertical forces give N=mg=50 N.
The limiting static friction is mu_s N=0.6(50)=30 N, and 12 N is within that limit.
answer.check: The actual friction must change if the applied pull changes while the block remains static; the 30 N value is only the maximum available.

hints.text: Because the block remains at rest, what horizontal force must friction balance?
Find the required static friction first; compare it with mu_s N only afterward.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the block with the 12 N pull, a friction arrow opposite it, the weight and the normal force. Label the friction f, not μ_s N.

questions.failure_signal: Your friction is 30 N: that is the most static friction can give, but a block at rest under a 12 N pull needs only 12 N; 30 N would drive it backward.

family_exposure.closure: Established: static friction takes whatever value rest requires, up to μ_s N; the limit is a ceiling, not the value. The transfer task tilts the push, so the ceiling itself changes with the force.

questions.stem: A 5 kg block is already sliding to the right on a horizontal floor. A constant 18 N horizontal force pulls it to the right. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20 and take g=10 m/s^2. Find the acceleration.
conditions: Relative sliding is already established.
The applied force is horizontal.

answer.summary: The block accelerates at 1.6 m/s^2 to the right.
reasoning: The vertical force balance gives N=mg=50 N.
Because the block is sliding, kinetic friction has magnitude mu_k N=0.20(50)=10 N and points left, opposite the relative sliding.
The horizontal net force is 18-10=8 N to the right.
Newton's second law gives a=8/5=1.6 m/s^2 to the right.
answer.check: The kinetic model is justified by the stated sliding; no static-friction feasibility test is needed for this already-sliding state.

hints.text: The contact state is already given: which friction model belongs to established sliding?
Find N first, then f_k=mu_k N, set its direction opposite the sliding, and apply Newton II.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the sliding block with the 18 N pull to the right, its weight and normal force, and a kinetic-friction arrow pointing opposite the sliding.

questions.failure_signal: Your acceleration is 3.6 m/s² (18/5, friction left out) or 5.6 m/s² (friction added to the pull): kinetic friction of 10 N acts against the sliding and must be subtracted.

family_exposure.closure: Established: once sliding is given, friction is fixed at μ_k N opposite the sliding, and Newton II gives the acceleration. The transfer task moves the applied force onto one block of a stacked pair, so the no-slip test has to be rebuilt.

questions.stem: A runner accelerates forward without the shoe slipping on the ground. Determine the direction of the static friction force exerted by the ground on the shoe, and justify it from the relative slip tendency at the contact.

Static friction opposes that relative slip tendency.
Therefore the ground exerts forward friction on the shoe, helping accelerate the runner forward.
answer.check: The friction direction may be the same as the runner's ground-frame velocity; the defining comparison is the contact-level relative slip tendency.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is pushed on a rough horizontal floor by a force P directed at an angle theta below the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Derive the largest P for which the block can remain at rest.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
The block remains in contact with the floor.
Assume cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta) > 0.

answer.summary: At impending slip, N=mg+P sin(theta) and P cos(theta)=mu_s N, so P_max = mu_s m g / (cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta)).
reasoning: The downward component of P increases the normal reaction, so the vertical balance gives N=mg+P sin(theta).
For a static state, friction must oppose the horizontal push; the maximum available value is reached only at impending slip.
At the threshold, P cos(theta)=mu_s[mg+P sin(theta)].
Rearranging gives P[cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta)]=mu_s mg and hence the stated P_max.
answer.check: Setting theta=0 reduces the result to P_max=mu_s mg, the ordinary horizontal-push threshold.

rubric.criterion: Computes N from the vertical force balance including the downward component of P.
rubric.evidence_of: Does not assume N=mg.

rubric.criterion: Uses static-friction equality only at impending slip.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishes a threshold condition from an unconditional friction law.

questions.stem: A block of mass m rests on a block of mass M on a smooth floor. A horizontal force F is applied to the upper block m. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is mu_s. Derive the largest F for which the blocks move together without slipping.
conditions: The lower block has no other horizontal contact force from the floor.
The contact between the two blocks remains horizontal.

answer.summary: If the blocks move together, a=F/(m+M). The lower block needs friction f_required=Ma. With N=mg at the interface, no slip requires MF/(m+M) <= mu_s m g, so F_max = mu_s m g (m+M)/M.
reasoning: Under the no-slip assumption, treat both blocks as one system to obtain the common acceleration a=F/(m+M).
Now isolate the lower block M. Its only horizontal force is the friction from the upper block, so f_required=Ma=MF/(m+M).
The interface normal is N=mg because the upper block has no vertical acceleration or other vertical force.
Static contact is feasible only while f_required <= mu_s N; equality gives the threshold F_max.
answer.check: The friction needed to accelerate the lower block is the quantity tested against the static limit; using f=mu_s N for every smaller F would erase the dependence on F.

questions.stem: Blocks A and B are side by side on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B and no adhesive connection. Compare two cases. In case 1 a horizontal force pushes A to the right into B and contact is maintained. In case 2 the same force pulls A to the left, away from B. In which case may one common horizontal acceleration be imposed, and why?
conditions: The contact force is an ordinary normal force and cannot pull the blocks together.
The floor is frictionless.

answer.summary: A common acceleration is justified in case 1 while maintained contact fixes the separation. It is not justified in case 2: the normal contact cannot pull B after A is pulled away, so the contact constraint is lost.
reasoning: Common acceleration must be earned from an active constraint that fixes relative separation.
When A is pushed into B and contact is maintained, the normal interaction can enforce the shared motion.
When A is pulled away from B, an ordinary normal force cannot act as a tensile connector to keep them together.
After separation, each block's acceleration must be obtained from its own remaining forces.
answer.check: If a proposed case-2 solution assigns a nonzero pulling normal force on B to preserve contact, it has given an ordinary contact force a capability it does not have.

hints.text: What physical condition must stay active before equal acceleration can be imposed?

hint_ladder.text: For each case, draw the two blocks and an arrow for how the force moves A. Mark whether A presses into B or moves away from it.

questions.failure_signal: You gave both cases the acceleration F/(m_A + m_B): in case 2 that would need an ordinary contact to pull B along, and a contact can only push.

questions.stem: Masses m_A and m_B, with m_B > m_A, hang from the two ends of one taut massless inextensible string over one fixed frictionless massless pulley. Derive the acceleration magnitude a and the common string tension T. State explicitly why T is not equal to either hanging weight during the acceleration.
conditions: Mass A accelerates upward and mass B accelerates downward.
Use the same acceleration magnitude a for the two ends, as required by the fixed string-length constraint.
Neglect air resistance.

answer.summary: The acceleration magnitude is a=(m_B-m_A)g/(m_A+m_B), and the common tension is T=2m_A m_B g/(m_A+m_B). During the motion T>m_A g and T<m_B g, so it is not equal to either weight unless the corresponding acceleration is zero.
reasoning: The fixed inextensible string gives equal acceleration magnitudes for the two ends while the ideal string/pulley model licenses one common tension T.
For A, upward positive gives T-m_A g=m_A a.
For B, downward positive gives m_B g-T=m_B a.
Adding the equations gives a=(m_B-m_A)g/(m_A+m_B).
Substitution into either body equation gives T=2m_A m_B g/(m_A+m_B).
Because A accelerates upward, its tension exceeds m_A g; because B accelerates downward, its tension is below m_B g.
answer.check: If m_A=m_B, the formula reduces to a=0 and T=mg, recovering the equilibrium special case.

hints.text: Separate the two claims you need: what fixes the acceleration relationship, and what licenses one common tension magnitude?
Write one signed Newton-II equation for each mass, then add the equations to eliminate T.

hint_ladder.text: Draw one diagram per mass, with the tension up and the weight down on each, and mark A's acceleration up and B's down.

questions.failure_signal: Your tension is m_A g or m_B g: while the masses accelerate, the string pulls A harder than A's weight and pulls B less than B's weight.

family_exposure.closure: Established: the fixed string length gives equal acceleration magnitudes, the ideal pulley gives one T, and each mass's own equation places T between the two weights. The transfer task makes the pulley heavy, so these two claims have to be separated.

questions.stem: Two blocks A and B are initially touching on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B. A horizontal force F is suddenly applied to A toward the left, away from B. A proposed solution treats A+B as one connected system and writes a=F/(m_A+m_B). Decide whether that model is valid immediately after the force is applied. If it is not, state the two accelerations.
conditions: There is no glue, string, or other connector.
The contact is an ordinary normal interaction that cannot pull.
Take rightward as positive.

answer.summary: The common-acceleration model is invalid because the force makes A separate from B and an ordinary normal contact cannot pull them together. Immediately after contact is lost, a_A=-F/m_A and a_B=0.
reasoning: The earlier common-acceleration rule applies only while an active condition fixes the blocks' separation.
Here F drives A away from B, so maintaining contact would require a tensile contact force on B, which an ordinary normal interaction cannot supply.
Once the contact force becomes zero, B has no horizontal force and therefore zero horizontal acceleration.
A has the applied leftward force F, so with rightward positive its acceleration is -F/m_A.
answer.check: The rejected value F/(m_A+m_B) would require B to accelerate left even though no horizontal interaction remains on B.

The pulley is now stated to have appreciable rotational inertia, and no rotational-dynamics relation is supplied. A student claims that both T_A=T_B and a_A+a_B=0 must either survive together or fail together. Decide which statement can still be obtained from the bounded material, and which statement is no longer licensed.
conditions: Coordinates y_A and y_B are measured positive away from the fixed pulley along the two straight string segments.

That geometric argument does not use equality of tension magnitudes.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is released from rest on a smooth fixed plane inclined at angle theta above the horizontal. Choose axes that make the contact constraint simple, determine the normal reaction, and find the block's acceleration along the plane.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.

answer.summary: Using axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane, weight has components mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane. Maintained contact gives N=mg cos(theta), and the tangential equation gives acceleration g sin(theta) down the plane.
reasoning: Choose the block and use +parallel down the plane and +perpendicular outward from the plane.
The physical forces are weight mg and the normal reaction N.
Resolve weight into mg sin(theta) parallel down the plane and mg cos(theta) perpendicular into the plane.
Maintained contact gives a_perp=0, so N-mg cos(theta)=0.
Along the plane, mg sin(theta)=m a_parallel, so a_parallel=g sin(theta) down the plane.
answer.check: At theta=0 the tangential acceleration tends to zero and N tends to mg; as theta approaches 90 degrees, N tends to zero and the tangential acceleration tends to g.

questions.stem: A block rests on a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Determine the friction required for rest and derive the condition under which the static state is possible.
conditions: No other force acts on the block.
The block is tested for rest; do not assume limiting friction at the start.

answer.summary: For rest, N=mg cos(theta) and static friction must act up the plane with required magnitude mg sin(theta). Rest is feasible when mg sin(theta) <= mu_s mg cos(theta), equivalently tan(theta) <= mu_s.
reasoning: Without friction the block tends to slide down the plane, so static friction required for rest points up the plane.
The perpendicular equation gives N=mg cos(theta).
The no-slip tangential equation requires f_required=mg sin(theta).
Static contact is possible only if f_required <= mu_s N.
Cancelling mg cos(theta)>0 gives tan(theta)<=mu_s.
answer.check: The calculation uses equality f_s=mu_s N only at the limiting angle; for a smaller angle the actual static friction is below its maximum.

conditions: The sliding direction is down the plane.
No other force acts on the block.
The plane is fixed.

reasoning: Maintained contact gives N=mg cos(theta).
Because the block is sliding down relative to the plane, kinetic friction points up the plane.
With down-plane positive, m a=mg sin(theta)-mu_k mg cos(theta).
Divide by m to obtain a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].

Resolve the horizontal force into P cos(theta) uphill and P sin(theta) into the plane.
Resolve weight into mg sin(theta) downhill and mg cos(theta) into the plane.
Maintained contact gives N-mg cos(theta)-P sin(theta)=0.
The parallel equation is P cos(theta)-mg sin(theta)=m a_parallel.
answer.check: At P=0 the result reduces to the ordinary smooth-incline equations, with negative uphill acceleration -g sin(theta).

For plane-aligned equations it may be represented by the components mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane, but the original mg must not also be added as a separate force in those component sums.
reasoning: A free-body inventory is a list of physical interactions acting on the chosen body.
Gravity is one Earth-on-block interaction, represented by the vector mg.
Resolving that vector into parallel/perpendicular components changes its coordinate description only.
The component equations may use the two components instead of the unresolved weight vector; they are not two new agents.
answer.check: The physical-force count remains two in this smooth-contact case: weight and normal reaction.

questions.stem: The same smooth fixed-incline problem is solved by two students. Student A uses axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane. Student B keeps horizontal/vertical laboratory axes. Decide whether both coordinate choices are physically valid, and explain why Student A's choice usually makes the contact constraint and acceleration easier to express.
conditions: Both students use one consistent inertial frame.
The plane is fixed and smooth.
No numerical angle is required.

answer.summary: Both coordinate systems are valid if used consistently. Plane-aligned axes are usually simpler because maintained contact becomes a_perp=0 and the unknown acceleration has only a parallel component; horizontal/vertical axes require projecting both the normal force and the constrained acceleration.

In plane-aligned axes, the normal reaction lies on the perpendicular axis and the tangential motion lies on the parallel axis.
The contact condition is therefore stated directly as a_perp=0.
In horizontal/vertical axes the same normal and acceleration must be represented by components, which is valid but algebraically less direct.

questions.stem: A block is at rest on a rough incline. A controllable force P acts up the plane. In one trial P is slightly smaller than mg sin(theta); in another it is slightly larger than mg sin(theta), and in both trials the available static friction is sufficient to prevent motion. The block remains at rest in both stated trials.
P acts exactly parallel to the plane.

Compare the applied uphill force P with the downhill gravity component mg sin(theta).
If gravity's component is larger, friction must act uphill to maintain rest.
If P is larger, friction must act downhill.
If the two non-friction tangential forces balance exactly, no tangential friction is required.

rubric.evidence_of: Applies the contact-level friction-direction rule.

rubric.evidence_of: Responds correctly to the reversed tangential tendency.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is held at rest on a rough fixed plane that rises to the right at angle theta. A horizontal force P pushes to the right. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Derive the condition on P and theta for the block to be able to remain at rest.

The applied force is horizontal.

The perpendicular rest condition gives N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta).
The tangential rest equation P cos(theta)+f_s-mg sin(theta)=0 gives the signed required friction f_required=mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta).
Do not choose a friction direction separately; the sign of f_required supplies it.
The static model is feasible when the magnitude of that required value does not exceed mu_s N.

questions.stem: A proposed plane-aligned solution writes the tangential force sum as mg + mg sin(theta) and the perpendicular force sum as N - mg - mg cos(theta). The solver says the component terms were added because the weight was resolved. Identify the modelling error and write the correct role of the weight in the two component equations.
conditions: The block is on a smooth fixed incline.
Only gravity and the normal reaction act.

answer.summary: The solution double-counts the same weight vector. In plane-aligned equations, gravity contributes mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane; the unresolved mg is not added again. Thus the tangential gravity term is mg sin(theta), and the perpendicular equation uses N-mg cos(theta)=0 for maintained contact.
reasoning: Weight mg is one physical force, not three.
Resolving it replaces its representation in the chosen component equations.
The original vector magnitude mg is not itself a signed scalar component along either tilted axis.
Use the two appropriate components in the two equations and keep the normal as the separate contact force.
answer.check: The corrected equations account for exactly two physical interactions: Earth-on-block gravity and plane-on-block normal contact.

rubric.criterion: Identifies double-counting of gravity as the error.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and travels the same distance s down the same incline of angle theta in two trials. On a smooth surface the time is t_0. On a rough surface the block slides throughout and the time is t > t_0. Assuming kinetic friction coefficient mu_k is constant, derive mu_k in terms of theta, t_0 and t.
conditions: Both trials start from rest at the same point.
The incline angle and travel distance are unchanged.
The rough-surface trial has established downward sliding with constant mu_k.

answer.summary: Smooth acceleration is a_0=g sin(theta), rough acceleration is a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)]. Since s=(1/2)at^2 from rest, a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2. Therefore mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].
reasoning: The smooth trial gives a_0=g sin(theta).
The rough sliding trial gives a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].
Equal distance from rest gives s=(1/2)a_0 t_0^2=(1/2)a t^2, hence a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2.
Substitute the two incline accelerations and solve for mu_k.
This yields mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].
answer.check: Because t>t_0, the bracket is positive. If t approaches t_0, the inferred mu_k approaches zero.

rubric.criterion: Builds the smooth and rough incline accelerations from the corresponding force models.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps the contact-state physics distinct between trials.

rubric.criterion: Uses equal-distance constant-acceleration kinematics to relate a/a_0 to t_0^2/t^2.
rubric.evidence_of: Connects the NLM result to the measured timing representation.

rubric.criterion: Solves to mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2] and checks its limiting sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Completes the cross-topic reasoning and verifies plausibility.

adaptation.reason: Changes a direct rough-incline acceleration derivation into an inference from smooth-versus-rough travel times over the same distance, requiring the NLM result to be connected to constant-acceleration kinematics.

hints.text: The two trials cover the same distance from rest. What relation connects distance, constant acceleration and travel time in each trial?
Express the rough acceleration from the friction model and the smooth acceleration from the no-friction model, then eliminate the common distance.

transfer.statement: The learner must combine the established rough-incline dynamics with an independent timing representation to infer the friction coefficient, rather than being asked directly for acceleration.
transfer.invariant: The rough-slope acceleration g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) and the smooth-slope g sin θ still hold; what changes is that μ_k must be inferred from travel times instead of being used to find an acceleration.

entry_needs: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing; the specific turning-point diagnostic from Motion is not a prerequisite.
learner_actions: Separate motion from change of motion.
Keep individual forces distinct from their net result.
Assign each force to the body on which it acts.
Determine friction direction from relative slip tendency.
Use signed net external force with F_net = m a.
Test static friction against its limit before using a limiting or kinetic formula.
Apply a common acceleration only when an active connection keeps the relevant separation fixed.
Use one common tension magnitude only under explicit ideal-string/redirection assumptions.
Derive the one-fixed-pulley acceleration relation from constant string length rather than a pulley-count rule.
Keep Newton-third-law partner forces on different bodies.
Use observer-frame/pseudo-force reasoning only when an explicit extension question demands it.
help_plan: Use a released low-friction cart for the first-law contrast.

application_contexts.title: Block on a fixed inclined plane
application_contexts.description: A rigid plane at angle theta to the horizontal used as an application context for body-specific FBDs, contact-aligned axes, force decomposition, Newton II, normal reaction and friction-state reasoning.
invariants: The plane is fixed unless a question explicitly states otherwise.
One may choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane without changing the physical forces.
For maintained contact with a fixed plane, the body's acceleration perpendicular to the plane is zero.
The normal reaction is determined by the perpendicular dynamics; it is not automatically mg.
If friction is present, its direction and model are determined from relative sliding or slip tendency at the contact.
